chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: The men quickly found their horses in the half-darkness, tightened saddle girths, and formed into companies. Denisov stood by the watchman's hut, giving final orders. The detachment's infantry filed along the road and quickly vanished among the trees in the mist of early dawn, hundreds of feet splashing through the mud. The esaul gave orders to his men. Petya held his horse by the bridle, impatiently awaiting the command to mount. His face, freshly washed in cold water, was glowing, and his eyes were especially bright. Cold shivers ran down his spine and his whole body pulsed rhythmically.
'Well, is everything ready?' asked Denisov. 'Bring the horses.'

The horses were brought. Denisov scolded the Cossack because the saddle girths were too loose, then mounted. Petya put his foot in the stirrup. His horse, out of habit, made as if to nip his leg, but Petya leaped quickly into the saddle, unaware of his own weight, and turning to look at the hussars moving up in the darkness behind him, rode up to Denisov.
'Vasili Dmitrich, give me something to do! Please... for God's sake!' he said.
Denisov seemed to have forgotten Petya even existed. He turned to glance at him.
'I ask one thing of you,' he said sternly, 'obey me and don't push yourself into anything.'

He didn't say another word to Petya the entire ride. When they reached the forest's edge, it was noticeably getting lighter over the field. Denisov whispered with the esaul, and the Cossacks began riding past Petya and Denisov. When they had all gone by, Denisov spurred his horse and rode down the hill. Slipping and sliding on their haunches, the horses carried their riders down into the ravine. Petya rode beside Denisov, the pulse of excitement in his body growing constantly stronger. It was getting lighter and lighter, but the mist still hid distant objects. Reaching the valley, Denisov looked back and nodded to a Cossack beside him.
'The signal!' he said.
The Cossack raised his arm, and a shot rang out. Instantly the sound of galloping hooves was heard, shouts broke out from all sides, and more shots followed.

At the first sound of pounding hooves and shouting, Petya whipped his horse and let the reins go slack, galloping forward without heeding Denisov, who yelled after him. It seemed to Petya that at the instant the shot was fired, it suddenly became as bright as noon. He galloped toward the bridge. Cossacks were racing along the road ahead of him. On the bridge he crashed into a Cossack who had fallen behind, but galloped on. In front of him, soldiers—probably French—were running from right to left across the road. One of them fell in the mud under his horse's hooves.

Cossacks were crowding around a hut, doing something. From the middle of the crowd came terrible screams. Petya galloped up, and the first thing he saw was the pale face and trembling jaw of a Frenchman clutching the shaft of a lance aimed at him.
'Hurrah!... Boys!... Ours!' shouted Petya, and giving his excited horse free rein, he galloped forward along the village street.

He could hear gunfire ahead. Cossacks, hussars, and ragged Russian prisoners who had come running from both sides of the road were shouting something loudly and incoherently. A dashing-looking Frenchman in a blue overcoat, bareheaded and with a frowning red face, had been fighting off the hussars. By the time Petya galloped up, the Frenchman had already fallen. 'Too late again!' flashed through Petya's mind, and he galloped on toward the place where the rapid gunfire was coming from. The shots came from the yard of the landowner's house he had visited the night before with Dolokhov. The French were making a stand behind a wattle fence in a garden thick with bushes, firing at the Cossacks crowding at the gate. Through the smoke, as he approached, Petya saw Dolokhov, his face a pale greenish tint, shouting to his men. 'Go around! Wait for the infantry!' he yelled as Petya rode up.
'Wait?... Hurrah!' shouted Petya, and without pausing for an instant, he galloped toward the place where the gunfire was thickest and the smoke was densest.

A volley rang out. Some bullets whistled past; others smacked into something. The Cossacks and Dolokhov galloped after Petya through the gateway into the courtyard. In the dense, wavering smoke, some of the French threw down their weapons and ran out of the bushes to meet the Cossacks, while others fled down the hill toward the pond. Petya was galloping across the courtyard, but instead of holding the reins, he was waving both arms about rapidly and strangely, slipping further and further to one side of his saddle. His horse, having galloped up to a campfire smoldering in the morning light, stopped suddenly, and Petya fell heavily onto the wet ground. The Cossacks saw his arms and legs jerk rapidly, though his head was completely still. A bullet had pierced his skull.

After speaking to the senior French officer—who came out of the house with a white handkerchief tied to his sword, announcing their surrender—Dolokhov dismounted and went over to Petya, who lay motionless with his arms flung out.
'Done for!' he said with a frown, and walked to the gate to meet Denisov, who was riding toward him.
'Killed?' cried Denisov, recognizing from a distance the unmistakable, horribly familiar posture of Petya's lifeless body.

'Done for!' Dolokhov repeated, as if saying the words gave him a kind of grim satisfaction, and he walked quickly to the prisoners, who were surrounded by Cossacks. 'We won't be taking them!' he called out to Denisov.
Denisov didn't reply. He rode up to Petya, dismounted, and with trembling hands turned toward himself the bloodstained, mud-covered face that had already gone white.

'I like having something sweet. Raisins—wonderful ones... take them all!' The words came back to him. And the Cossacks looked around in surprise at the sound—like the yelp of a dog—with which Denisov turned away, walked to the wattle fence, and gripped it.
Among the Russian prisoners rescued by Denisov and Dolokhov was Pierre Bezukhov.
